subject: Bank of Canada may hike into 6.5% unemployment
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a mortgage renewal coming, a line of credit, or savings parked in a GIC, Wednesday morning is worth your attention. The Bank of Canada announces at 9:45 am Toronto time, and for the first time in a year the betting is on a rate increase instead of a hold.

## What moved this week

The **overnight rate**, the rate the Bank sets for banks lending to each other for one night, has sat at 2.25 per cent for about a year. As recently as the Friday before last, swap markets gave a Wednesday increase roughly 30 per cent odds. The Globe and Mail reported that by Monday those odds had jumped to about 80 per cent, and they held near there all week. Two things did it. Governor Tiff Macklem, speaking at the IMF meetings the weekend before, said he expects the Bank to revise its inflation forecast higher, and Bloomberg reported Friday that he is seeing more evidence that high oil prices are feeding Canadian growth. Then Statistics Canada reported Monday that inflation ran at 3.1 per cent in September, up from 3.0 per cent in August. A Reuters poll taken Wednesday through Friday found 56 per cent of 34 economists now expect a move to 2.50 per cent.

## Gasoline is doing almost all of the work

Here is why I think raising would be the wrong call. Nearly all of that 3.1 per cent is gas. Statistics Canada put gasoline up 27.8 per cent from a year earlier, pushed by the Middle East conflict, and with gas stripped out inflation was 2.2 per cent in September, down from 2.4 per cent in August. The Bank's own preferred gauges of **core inflation**, which drop the most extreme price moves to show the underlying trend, came in at 1.8 per cent for CPI-trim and 1.9 per cent for CPI-median. Both sit under the Bank's 2 per cent target. Prices rose 0.1 per cent on the month. A central bank cannot drill an oil well. Making Canadians borrow at higher cost does nothing about a crude shock from the other side of the world, it just charges us rent while that shock passes through.

## The labour market is already bending

The economy underneath this is not strong. Statistics Canada's September labour report, out October 9, showed employment down 68,000 and unemployment up to 6.5 per cent. Public sector employment fell by 70,000. Workers aged 15 to 24 lost 48,000 jobs, which is the line I keep rereading, because that is roughly my cohort walking into next summer's hiring. The three-month trend has turned negative, averaging a loss of close to 12,000 jobs a month. Shoppers are holding up better. Retail sales rose 1.2 per cent in August to $74.6 billion, Statistics Canada reported Friday, with all nine subsectors up and volumes up 1.2 per cent, so people bought more goods rather than just pricier ones. The early read on September points to another 0.7 per cent. Decent spending, shrinking payrolls.

## The takeaway

Watch 9:45 am Wednesday, then read the Monetary Policy Report that lands with it instead of the headline. What I want to know is whether the Bank raises its inflation forecast while conceding core is below 2 per cent, because that would tell me it is answering to oil and to market pricing rather than to demand at home. If you renew a mortgage in the next six months, call your lender this week, ask what a quarter point does to the payment, and take a rate hold if one is offered. If the Bank holds after all, expect the loonie to hand back some of last week's gain, when it touched a one-month high.
